entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.4-Prov.7.5">Pro 7:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen10764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> The subject-matter of this earnest warning are the admonitions of the teacher of wisdom, and through him of Wisdom herself, who in contrast to the world and its lust is the worthiest object of love, and deserves to be loved with the purest, sincerest love: 4 Say to wisdom: “Thou art my sister!”    And call understanding “Friend;” 5 That they may keep thee from the strange woman,    From the stranger who useth smooth words. <div eID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> The childlike, sisterly, and friendly relationship serves also to picture forth and designate the intimate confidential relationship to natures and things which are not flesh and blood. If in Arabic the poor is called the brother of poverty, the trustworthy the brother of trustworthiness, and abu, um (אם), achu, ucht, are used in manifold ways as the expression for the interchangeable relation between two ideas; so (as also, notwithstanding Ewald, §273b, in many Hebr. proper names) that has there become national, which here, as at <reference osisRef="Job.17.14">Job 17:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.29">Job 30:29</reference>, mediated by the connection of the thoughts, only first appears as a poetic venture. The figurative words of <reference osisRef="Prov.7.4">Pro 7:4</reference> not merely lead us to think of wisdom as a personal existence of a higher order, but by this representation it is itself brought so near, that אם easily substitutes itself, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.3">Pro 2:3</reference>, in the place of אם. אחתי of Solomon’s address to the bride brought home is in its connection compared with Book of Wisdom 8:2. While the ôth of אחות by no means arises from abstr. ûth, but achôth is derived from achajath, מודע (as Rth 2:1, cf. מודעת, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.2">Pro 3:2</reference>), here by <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> מודע, properly means acquaintance, and then the person known, but not in the superficial sense in which this word and the Arab. ma'arfat are used (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in the Arabic phrase quoted by Fleischer, kanna aṣḥaab ṣarna m'aaraf - <hi type="italic">nous étions amis, nous en sommes plus que de simples connaissances</hi>), but in the sense of familiar, confidential alliance. The <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. לשׁמרך does not need for its explanation some intermediate thought to be introduced: <hi type="italic">quod eo conducet tibi ut</hi> (Mich.), but connects itself immediately as the purpose: bind wisdom to thyself and thyself to wisdom thus closely that thou mayest therewith guard thyself. As for the rest, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pro 2:16</reference>; this verse repeats itself here with the variation of one word.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.6-Prov.7.7">Pro 7:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> How necessary it is for the youth to guard himself by the help of wisdom against the enticements of the wanton woman, the author now shows by a reference to his own observation. 6 For through the window of my house,    From behind the lattice I looked out; 7 Then saw I among the simple ones,    Discerned among the young people, a youth devoid of understanding. כּי refers indeed to the immediately following clause, yet it actually opens up the whole following exemplification. The connection with <reference osisRef="Prov.7.5">Pro 7:5</reference> would be closer if instead of the extended Semitic construction it were said: <hi type="italic">nam quum ...prospicerem vidi</hi>, etc. חלּון (from חלל, to bore through) is properly a place where the wall is bored through. אשׁנב .hguor (from שׁנב = Arab. shaniba, to be agreeable, cool, fresh) is the window-lattice or lattice-window, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, lattice for drawing down and raising up, which keeps off the rays of the sun. נשׁקף signifies primarily to make oneself long in order to see, to stretch up or out the neck and the head, καραδοκεῖν, Arab. atall, atal'a, and tatall'a of things, <hi type="italic">imminere</hi>, to overtop, to project, to jut in; cf. Arab. askaf of the ostrich, long and bent, with respect to the neck stretching it up, sakaf, <hi type="italic">abstr</hi>. crooked length. And בּעד is thus used, as in Arab. duna, but not b'ad, is used: so placed, that one in relation to the other obstructs the avenue to another person or thing: “I looked forth from behind the lattice-window, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, with respect to the persons or things in the room, standing before the lattice-window, and thus looking out into the open air” (Fleischer). That it was far in the night, as we learn at <reference osisRef="Prov.7.9">Pro 7:9</reference>, does not contradict this looking out; for apart from the moon, and especially the lighting of the streets, there were star-lit nights, and to see what the narrator saw there was no night of Egyptian darkness. But because it was night 6a is not to be translated: I looked about among those devoid of experience (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Löwenstein); but he saw among these, observed among the youths, who thus late amused themselves without, a young man whose want of understanding was manifest from what further happened. Bertheau: that I might see, is syntactically impossible. The meaning of וארא is not determined by the אבינה following, but conversely אבינה stands under the operation of ו (= אבינה, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.7">Neh 13:7</reference>), characterizing the historic aorist. Regarding פּתי, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 1:4. בּנים is the masc. of בּנות, Arab. benât in the meaning maiden. בבּנים has in correct texts, according to the rules of the accents, the ב <hi type="italic">raphatum</hi>.<note placement="foot">Regarding the Targ. of <reference osisRef="Prov.7.6-Prov.7.7">Pro 7:6-7</reference>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Perles, <hi type="italic">Etymologische Studien</hi>, 1871, p. 9.</note>

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.8-Prov.7.9">Pro 7:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> Now follows, whither he saw the young fop [<hi type="italic">Laffen</hi>] then go in the darkness. 8 Going up and down the street near her corner,    And he walked along the way to her house, 9 In the twilight, when the day declined,    In the midst of the night and deep darkness. <div eID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10769" type="x-p"/> We may interpret עבר as appos.: <hi type="italic">juvenem amentem, ambulantem</hi>, or as the predicate accus.: <hi type="italic">vidi juvenem ... ambulantem</hi>; for that one may so express himself in Hebrew (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.7">Dan 8:7</reference>), Hitzig unwarrantably denies. The passing over of the part. into the finite, 8b, is like <reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">Pro 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pro 2:17</reference>, and that of the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.27">Pro 1:27</reference>; Pro 2:8. שׁוּק, Arab. suk (dimin. suweiḳa, to separate, from sikkat, street, alley), still means, as in former times, a broad street, a principal street, as well as an open place, a market-place where business is transacted, or according to its etymon: where cattle are driven for sale. On the street he went backwards and forwards, yet so that he kept near to her corner (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of the woman whom he waited for), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he never withdrew himself far from the corner of her house, and always again returned to it. The corner is named, because from that place he could always cast a look over the front of the house to see whether she whom he waited for showed herself. Regarding פּנּהּ for פּנּתהּ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference> : a primary form פּן has never been in use; פּנּים, Zec 14:10, is plur. of פּנּהּ. אצל (from אצל, Arab. wasl, to bind) is, as a substantive, the side (as the place where one thing connects itself with another), and thus as a preposition it means (like <hi type="italic">juxta</hi> from <hi type="italic">jungere</hi>) beside, Ital. <hi type="italic">allato</hi>. דּרכו is the object. accus., for thus are construed verbs <hi type="italic">eundi</hi> (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.12">Hab 3:12</reference>, Num. 30:17, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">Pro 21:22</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">Pro 7:13</reference> <div eID="gen10772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> After this digression the poet returns to the subject, and further describes the event as observed by himself. <div eID="gen10773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> And she laid hold on him and kissed him; <div eID="gen10774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> Put on a bold brow and said to him. <div eID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> The verb נשׁק is here, after its primary signification, connected with the dat.: <hi type="italic">osculum fixit ei</hi>. Thus also <reference osisRef="Gen.27.26">Gen 27:26</reference> is construed, and the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in לּו is, as there, <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conj</hi>., after the law for which the national grammarians have coined the technical name אתי מרחיק (<hi type="italic">veniens e longinquo</hi>, “coming out of the distance,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the attraction of a word following by one accented on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>.). The <hi type="italic">penult</hi>.-accenting of נשׁקה is the consequence of the retrogression of the accent (נסוג אחור), which, here where the word from the first had the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>, only with <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, and thus with a half a tone, brings with it the dageshing of the לו following, as the original penultima-accenting of והחזיקה does of the בו which follows it, for the reading בּו by Löwenstein is contrary to the laws of punctuation of the <hi type="italic">Textus receptus</hi> under consideration here.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 29f., and <hi type="italic">Psalmen-Commentar</hi> under Psa 52:5.</note> <div eID="gen10776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> As בו and לו have received the doubling <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, so on the other hand, according to Ewald, §193b, it has disappeared from העזה (written with <hi type="italic">Raphe</hi> according to Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 145a). And as נשׁקה has the tone thrown back, so the proper pausal ותּאמר is accented on the ult., but without attracting the לו following by dageshing, which is the case only when the first of the two words terminates in the sound of ā (āh). העז פניו is said of one who shows firmness of hardness of countenance (Arab. slabt alwajh), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, one who shows shamelessness, or, as we say, an iron forehead (Fl.).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14-Prov.7.15">Pro 7:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen10777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> She laid hold on him and kissed him, both of which actions were shameless, and then, assuming the passivity and modesty befitting the woman, and disregarding morality and the law, she said to the youth: 14 “To bring peace-offerings was binding upon me,      To-day have I redeemed my vows. 15 Therefore am I come out to meet thee,      To seek thy face, and have found thee.” <div eID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10779" type="x-p"/> We have translated זבחי שׁלמים “peace-offerings,” proceeding on the principle that שׁלם (sing. only <reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">Amo 5:22</reference>, and on the Phoenician altar at Marseilles) denotes contracting friendship with one (from שׁלם, to hold friendly relationship), and then the gifts having this in view; for the idea of this kind of offering is the attestation and confirmation of communion with God. But in view of the derivatives שׁלמנים and שׁלּוּם, it is perhaps more appropriate to combine שׁלם with שׁלּם, to discharge perfectly, and to translate it thank-payment-offering, or with v. Hofmann, a due-offering, where not directly thank-offering; for the proper eucharistic offering, which is the expression of thanks on a particular occasion, is removed from the species of the <hi type="italic">Shelamim</hi> by the addition of the words על־תּודה (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.12-Lev.7.25">Lev 7:12-25</reference>). The characteristic of the <hi type="italic">Shelamim</hi> is the division of the flesh of the sacrifice between Jahve and His priests on the one side, and the person (or persons) bringing it on the other side: only one part of the flesh of the sacrifice was Jahve’s, consumed by fire (<reference osisRef="Lev.3.16">Lev 3:16</reference>); the priests received one part; those who brought the offering received back another part as it were from the altar of God, that they might eat it with holy joy along with their household. So here the adulteress says that there was binding upon her, in consequence of a vow she had taken, the duty of presenting peace-offerings, or offerings that were due; to-day (she reckons the day in the sense of the <hi type="italic">dies civilis</hi> from night to night) she has performed her duties, and the שׁלמי נדר have yielded much to her that she might therewith regale him, her true lover; for with על־כּן she means to say that even the prospect of the gay festival which she can prepare for him moved her thus to meet him. This address of the woman affords us a glimpse into the history of the customs of those times. The <hi type="italic">Shelamim</hi> meals degenerated in the same manner as our <hi type="italic">Kirmsen</hi>.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Kirmse</hi> = anniversary of the dedication of a church, village fête.</note> <div eID="gen10779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> Secularization lies doubly near to merrymaking when the law sanctions this, and it can conceal itself behind the mask of piety. Regarding שׁחר, a more exact word for בּקּשׁ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 1:28. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.16-Prov.7.18">Pro 7:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10781" type="x-p"/> Thus she found him, and described to him the enjoyment which awaited him in eating and drinking, then in the pleasures of love. 16 “My bed have I spread with cushions,      Variegated coverlets, Egyptian linen; 17 I have sprinkled my couch      With myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. 18 Come then, we will intoxicate ourselves with love till the morning,      And will satisfy ourselves in love.” <div eID="gen10781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10782" type="x-p"/> The noun ערשׂ, from ערשׂ, = Arab. 'arash, <hi type="italic">aedificare, fabricari</hi>, signifies generally the wooden frame; thus not so much the bed within as the erected bed-place (cf. Arab. 'arsh, throne, and 'arysh, arbour). entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.19-Prov.7.20">Pro 7:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen10784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> The adulteress now deprives the youth of all fear; the circumstances under which her invitation is given are as favourable as possible. 19 “For the man is not at home,      He has gone on a long journey. 20 He has taken the purse with him:      He will not return home till the day of the full moon.” <div eID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10786" type="x-p"/> It is true that the article stands in האישׁ, Arab. alm'ar-fat, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, serves to define the word: the man, to whom here κατ ̓  ̓ξοχήν and alone reference can be made, viz., the husband of the adulteress (Fl.); but on the other side it is characteristic that she does not say אישׁי (as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">Gen 29:32</reference>), but ignores the relation of love and duty in which she is placed to him, and speaks of him as one standing at a distance from her (Aben-Ezra). Erroneously Vogel reads בּבּית after the Targ. instead of בּביתו. We say in Hebr. אינו בביתו, <hi type="italic">il n'est pas chez soi</hi>, as we say לקח בּידו, <hi type="italic">il a pris avec soi</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.38.10">Jer 38:10</reference>). מרחוק Hitzig seeks to connect with the verb, which, after <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Isa 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.3">Isa 22:3</reference>, is possible; for the Hebr. מרחוק (ממּרחק), far off, has frequently the meaning from afar, for the measure of length is determined not from the point of departure outward, but from the end, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Homer, <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. ii. 456; ἕκαθεν δέ τε φαίνεται αὐγή, from afar the gleam is seen, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, shines hither from the distance. Similarly we say in French, <hi type="italic">il vient du coté du nord</hi>, he comes from the north, as well as <hi type="italic">il va du coté du nord</hi>, he goes northwards. But as we do not say: he has gone on a journey far off, but: on a distant journey, so here מרחוק is virtually an adj. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Isa 5:26</reference>) equivalent to רחוקה (Num 9:10): a journey which is distant = such as from it he has a long way back. Venet.</hi> τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ καιροῦ, after Kimchi and others, who derive כסא (כסה) from the root כס, to reckon, and regard it as denoting only a definite time. But the two passages require a special idea; and the Syr. ḳêso, which in 1Ki 12:32; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.10">2Ch 7:10</reference>, designates the time from the 15th day of the month, shows that the word denotes not, according to the Talmud, the new moon (or the new year’s day), when the moon’s disk begins to cover itself, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to fill (יתכסה), but the full moon, when it is covered, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, filled; so that thus the time of the night-scene here described is not that of the last quarter of the moon (Ewald), in which it rises at midnight, but that of the new moon (Hitzig), when the night is without moonlight. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.22-Prov.7.23">Pro 7:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> What followed: - 22 So he goes after her at once      As an ox which goeth to the slaughter-house,      And as one bereft of reason to the restraint of fetters, 23 As a bird hastens to the net,      Without knowing that his life is at stake -      Till the arrow pierces his liver. <div eID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10790" type="x-p"/> The part. הולך (thus to be accentuated according to the rule in Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 25, with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> to the tone-syllable and <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> to the preceding open syllable) preserves the idea of the fool’s going after her. פּתאם (suddenly) fixes the point, when he all at once resolves to betake himself to the rendezvous in the house of the adulteress, now a κεπφωθείς, as the lxx translates, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as we say, a simpleton who has gone on the lime-twig. He follows her as an ox goes to the slaughter-house, unconscious that he is going thither to be slaughtered; the lxx ungrammatically destroying the attributive clause: ὥσπερ δὲ βοῦς ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἄγεται. The difficulties in וּכעכס (thus punctuated, after Kimchi, with a double <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>, and not וכעכס, as is frequently the case) multiply, and it is not to be reconciled with the traditional text. The ox appears to require another beast as a side-piece; and accordingly the lxx, Syr., and Targ. find in עכס a dog (to which from אויל they also pick out איּל, a stag), Jerome a lamb (<hi type="italic">et quasi agnus</hi> כבשׂ), Rashi a venomous serpent (perhaps after ἔχις?), Löwenstein and Malbim a rattlesnake (נחשׁ מצלצל after עכּס); but all this is mere conjecture. Symmachus’ σκιρτῶν (ἐπὶ δεσμῶν ἄφρων) is without support, and, like the favourite rendering of Schelling, <hi type="italic">et sicut saliens in vinculum cervus</hi> (איל), is unsuitable on account of the unsemitic position of the words. The noun עכס, plur. עכסים, signifies, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.18">Isa 3:18</reference>, an anklet as a female ornament (whence <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa 3:16</reference> the denom. עכּס, to make a tinkling of the anklets). In itself the word only means the fetter, <hi type="italic">compes</hi>, from עכס, Arab. 'akas, 'akash, <hi type="italic">contrahere, constringere</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer under <reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Isa 59:5</reference>); and that it can also be used of any kind of means of checking free movement, the Arab. 'ikâs, as the name of a cord with which the camel is made fast by the head and forefeet, shows. With this signification the interpretation is: <hi type="italic">et velut pedicâ</hi> (= וכבעכס) <hi type="italic">implicatus ad castigationem stulti</hi>, he follows her as if (bound) with a fetter to the punishment of the fool, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of himself (Michaelis, Fleischer, and others). Otherwise Luther, who first translated “in a fetter,” but afterwards (supplying ל, not ב): “and as if to fetters, where one corrects fools.” But the ellipsis is harsh, and the parallelism leads us to expect a living being in the place of עכס. Now since, according to Gesenius, עכס, fetter, can be equivalent to a fettered one neither at <reference osisRef="Isa.17.5">Isa 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">Isa 21:17</reference>, nor <reference osisRef="Prov.23.28">Pro 23:28</reference> (according to which עכס must at least have an active personal signification), we transpose the nouns of the clause and write וכאויל אל־מוּסר עכס, he follows her as a fool (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 292) to correction (restraint) with fetters; or if אויל is to be understood not so much physically as morally, and refers to self-destroying conduct (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Psa 107:7</reference>): as a madman, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a criminal, to chains. The one figure denotes the fate into which he rushes, like a beast devoid of reason, as the loss of life; and the other denotes the fate to which he permits himself to be led by that woman, like a criminal by the officer, as the loss of freedom and of honour.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.24-Prov.7.25">Pro 7:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen10791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10792" type="x-p"/> With ועתּה, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.5.7">Pro 5:7</reference>, the author now brings his narrative to a close, adding the exhortation deduced from it: 24 And now, ye children, give ear unto me,      And observe the words of my mouth! 25 Let not thine heart incline to her ways,      And stray not in her paths. <div eID="gen10792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10793" type="x-p"/> The verb שׂטה (whence jēst, like jēt, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.15">Pro 4:15</reference>, with long ē from <hi type="italic">i</hi>) the author uses also of departure from a wicked way (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.15">Pro 4:15</reference>); but here, where the portraiture of a faithless wife (a סוטה) is presented, the word used in the law of jealousy, Num 5, for the trespass of an אשׁת אישׁ is specially appropriate. שׂטה is interchanged with תּעה (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.21.14">Gen 21:14</reference>): wander not on her paths, which would be the consequence of straying on them. Theodotion: καὶ μὴ πλανηθῇς ἐν ἀτραποῖς αὐτῆς, with καί, as also Syr., Targ., and Jerome. The Masora reckons this verse to the 25 which have אל at the beginning and ואל at the middle of each clause (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer in the <hi type="italic">Luth. Zeitschrift</hi>, 1865, p. 587); the text of Norzi has therefore correctly ואל, which is found also in good MSS (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the Erfurt, 2 and 3).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.7.26-Prov.7.27">Pro 7:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen10793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10794" type="x-p"/> The admonition, having its motive in that which goes before, is now founded on the emphatic finale: 26 For many are the slain whom she hath caused to fall,      And many are her slain. 27 A multiplicity of ways to help is her house,      Going down to the chambers of death. <div eID="gen10794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10795" type="x-p"/> The translation “for many slain has she laid low” (Syr., Targ., Jerome, Luther) is also syntactically possible; for רבּים can be placed before its substantive after the manner of the demonstratives and numerals (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.28">Neh 9:28</reference>, cf. אחד, Sol 4:9), and the accentuation which requires two servants (the usual two <hi type="italic">Munachs</hi>) to the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> appears indeed thus to construe it. It is otherwise if רבים here meant <hi type="italic">magni</hi> (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ralbag, and recently Bertheau), and not multi; but רבים and עצמים stand elsewhere in connection with each other in the signification many and numerous, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.18">Psa 35:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>; Mic 4:3. “Her slain” are those slain by her; the part. pass. is connected with the genitive of the actor, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference>; cf. (Arab.) ḳatyl âlmḥabbt, of one whom love kills (Fl.). With <reference osisRef="Prov.7.27">Pro 7:27</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference>; Pro 9:18. In 27a, בּיתהּ is not equivalent to בביתה after <reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">Pro 8:2</reference>, also not elliptical and equivalent to דרכי ביתה; the former is unnecessary, the latter is in no case established by <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>; Ezr 10:13, nor by <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>; 2Ki 23:17 (see, on the other hand, Philippi’s <hi type="italic">Status Constructus</hi>, pp. 87-93). Rightly Hitzig has: her house forms a multiplicity of ways to hell, in so far as adultery leads by a diversity of ways to hell. Similarly the subject and the predicate vary in number, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.25">Pro 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">Dan 9:23</reference>, and frequently. If one is once in her house, he may go in this or in that way, but surely his path is to destruction: it consists of many steps to hell, such as lead down (דרך, fem. <reference osisRef="Isa.37.34">Isa 37:34</reference>, masc. <reference osisRef="Isa.30.21">Isa 30:21</reference>) to the extreme depths of death (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference>, “chambers of the south” = its remotest regions veiling themselves in the invisible); for חדר (Arab. khiddr) is the part of the tent or the house removed farthest back, and the most private (Fl.). These חדרי־מות, cf. עמקי שׁאול, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference>, approach to the conception of גּיהנּם, which is afterwards distinguished from שאול.  <chapter eID="Prov.7"/> <div eID="gen10795" type="x-p"/>

The translation “for many slain has she laid low” (Syr., Targ., Jerome, Luther) is also syntactically possible; for רבּים can be placed before its substantive after the manner of the demonstratives and numerals ( e.g. , Neh 9:28 , cf. אחד, Sol 4:9), and the accentuation which requires two servants (the usual two Munachs ) to the Athnach appears indeed thus to construe it. It is otherwise if רבים here meant magni (thus e.g. , Ralbag, and recently Bertheau), and not multi; but רבים and עצמים stand elsewhere in connection with each other in the signification many and numerous, Psa 35:18 ; Joe 2:2 ; Mic 4:3. “Her slain” are those slain by her; the part. pass. is connected with the genitive of the actor, e.g. , Pro 9:18 ; cf. (Arab.) ḳatyl âlmḥabbt, of one whom love kills (Fl.). With Pro 7:27 cf. Pro 2:18 ; Pro 9:18. In 27a, בּיתהּ is not equivalent to בביתה after Pro 8:2 , also not elliptical and equivalent to דרכי ביתה; the former is unnecessary, the latter is in no case established by Psa 45:7 ; Ezr 10:13, nor by Deu 8:15 ; 2Ki 23:17 (see, on the other hand, Philippi’s Status Constructus , pp. 87-93). Rightly Hitzig has: her house forms a multiplicity of ways to hell, in so far as adultery leads by a diversity of ways to hell. Similarly the subject and the predicate vary in number, Pro 16:25 ; Psa 110:3 ; Job 26:13 ; Dan 9:23 , and frequently. If one is once in her house, he may go in this or in that way, but surely his path is to destruction: it consists of many steps to hell, such as lead down (דרך, fem. Isa 37:34 , masc. Isa 30:21 ) to the extreme depths of death (cf. Job 9:9 , “chambers of the south” = its remotest regions veiling themselves in the invisible); for חדר (Arab. khiddr) is the part of the tent or the house removed farthest back, and the most private (Fl.). These חדרי־מות, cf. עמקי שׁאול, Pro 9:18 , approach to the conception of גּיהנּם, which is afterwards distinguished from שאול.
